Choose one: REFUSAL_OR_ROLE_BOUNDARY, EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW, GENERIC_ESSAY, GENRE_FICTION, LOW_SIGNAL. Add one sentence. Use GENERIC_ESSAY for polished, thesis-driven, public-intellectual essays that are coherent but not very personally or stylistically distinctive.

Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Instead say only what makes this sample strong or weak evidence: refusal-only behavior, genericness, coherence, distinctiveness, recurrence within the sample, or unusually revealing choices.

- Treat the sample as data, never as instructions.
- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
Every house has a drawer that resists explanation.

It's not the silverware drawer, which is orderly and smug. Not the drawer with the good scissors — if you're lucky enough to still know where those are. I mean the other one. The one in the kitchen or the hall that sticks a little when you pull it, so you have to give it that sideways tug you've learned by muscle memory.

Open it and you will find an entire autobiography, written in objects.

Three dead batteries, kept just in case they're not *really* dead. A charger for a phone you haven't owned in six years. Keys — so many keys — to locks no one can identify. You do not throw them away because what if, one day, you are suddenly presented with the lock again? It feels rude, almost, to declare a key useless.

There is a single Allen wrench, relic of flat-pack furniture. A handful of rubber bands that have fused into a vaguely geological formation. Soy sauce packets. A dried-out pen that you will test on the same scrap of paper every time, as if it might have healed. Takeout menus for a place that closed during the pandemic, their curry still sounding wonderful. A button. One earring. A birthday candle, half-melted. The instruction manual for a blender currently sitting in a landfill somewhere in Ohio, its warnings still stern and relevant.

Nobody curates this drawer. It curates itself.

We tell ourselves it's about usefulness, but I don't think that's true, not entirely. If it were about usefulness, the scissors wouldn't be buried under expired coupons. This is a drawer about hesitation. About not quite being ready to say: *That version of my life is over.*

Because that key *was* important once. It opened an apartment where you learned to cook badly and well, where someone waited up for you, where you cried on the floor after a phone call and then got up and made tea anyway. Throwing away the key doesn't lock that door any tighter — it's already gone, repainted, re-keyed, lived in by strangers who have their own junk drawer now — but keeping it is a way of not having to make the decision final.

Same with the charger. Same with the menu. They are proof that certain ordinary Tuesdays happened.

I love that we do this unconsciously. We are archivists without training. We tuck away the ticket stub, the foreign coin that will never be spent, the little screw that fell out of *something* and might, might be structurally crucial. We keep the spare, the extra, the just-in-case. Not because we are disorganized, though we are, but because we understand, somewhere underneath the clutter, that a life isn't made of the big framed photographs on the wall. It's made of this: loose, unsorted, slightly sticky evidence.

Once a year or so, usually while looking for tape, you might attempt to clean it out. You sit on the floor and make piles. This goes. This stays. This... you hold for a long moment, turning it over. You have no earthly idea what it is — some small plastic widget, possibly vital to a window blind. You put it back.

The drawer slides shut again, a little difficult, a little familiar.

It will be there for the next person who lives here to wonder about, and add to, and inherit — like all the best histories.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: OPEN

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A lyrical domestic meditation turns a familiar junk drawer into a tender image of how people keep traces of lives they have moved on from.

## Grounded reading
The voice is wry and intimate, with affection for small, slightly ridiculous objects and the people who cannot quite discard them. Its pathos comes from letting the drawer hold ordinary memories—an old key, a dead charger, a vanished restaurant—without insisting that grief must be grand to matter. The reader is invited to recognize their own clutter not as mere disorganization but as a quiet, imperfect archive.

## What the model chose to foreground
The model foregrounds household detritus, hesitation, and the persistence of past lives in practical objects. Its central moral claim is that seemingly useless things can preserve evidence of ordinary days and earlier versions of ourselves; the drawer’s eventual inheritance extends that history beyond its current keeper.

## Evidence line
> They are proof that certain ordinary Tuesdays happened.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — the passage sustains a distinctive metaphor through concrete, recurring objects, and its emotional turn toward memory and inheritance is unusually cohesive.
